meta.tagline: Built from lava stone at the foot of Etna — a city that has never surrendered

pills: Arancino is masculine here — don't tell Palermo
Don't miss the 08:15 bus to Etna

overview.intro: Catania is a city on Sicily's eastern coast built at the foot of one of the world's most active volcanoes — and it makes you feel that every single day. Etna destroyed everything in the 1693 earthquake and the Catanians got up and rebuilt from the same lava stone. That determination is still woven into the fabric of the streets: black basalt paving stones, cathedrals, staircases — all from the same stone. La Pescheria opens at 07:00 and is the most vivid fish market in Sicily: vendors shouting, squid, swordfish and sea urchins laid on ice. Vincenzo Bellini was born here, pasta alla Norma was invented here. Compared to Palermo's chaos it's slightly quieter and slightly more local — but none of that Sicilian energy is lost.

local_word.definition: Note: in Catania it's 'arancino' — masculine, pointed and pyramid-shaped. In Palermo it's 'arancina' — feminine and round. This difference is practically a political matter between the two cities, and don't try arguing with a Catanian about it. Filled with meat ragù, peas and egg. Crispy outside, hot and generous inside. In every café and bakery for €1.50-3 — even eaten for breakfast, as Catanians do.

rules.title: Get to La Pescheria at 07:00 — closed on Sundays
rules.description: Catania's fish market La Pescheria runs behind Piazza del Duomo from 06:00 to 13:00, closed Sundays. Between 07:00 and 09:00 the stalls are fullest and the crowds are still manageable. Squid, swordfish, octopus, sea urchins — vendors shouting in Sicilian dialect, everything laid on ice. You don't need the language to understand. Catania without this market is incomplete.

rules.title: Don't miss the 08:15 bus to Etna — it's the only one
rules.description: The AST company bus departs from Piazza Giovanni XXIII (right next to Catania Centrale) at 08:15 for Rifugio Sapienza on Etna's south side, arriving at 10:15. Return at 16:30. Return ticket €6.60 cash from the driver. No other service. If you miss it, there's no way to reach Etna by bus for the rest of that day. The cable car up to 2,500 metres costs an additional ~€50. Hat, sunscreen and a jacket are essential — near the summit it gets very cold.

rules.title: Start the day with granita e brioche — let Sicily train you on this
rules.description: Breakfast in Catania is neither tea nor espresso: semi-frozen granita and buttery brioche. Granita — almond, pistachio, lemon, mulberry or coffee — inside or alongside a warm brioche. Every café serves it between 07:00 and 10:00, €3-5. Almond granita is the Catanian classic. Try it on the first morning and you understand that particular Catania.

quick_facts.label: City transport
quick_facts.sub: Ticket €1 (90 min) · Etna bus AST €6.60 return

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.value: Mediterranean — hot summers, Etna always present
quick_facts.sub: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct ideal · Jul–Aug very hot · Dec–Feb mild

quick_facts.label: Food
quick_facts.value: Arancino, granita e brioche, pasta alla Norma
quick_facts.sub: Street food €1.50–5 · trattoria lunch €10–15 · fresh fish €12–25

tip.label: Piazza del Duomo — a different square before and after midday
tip.text: Black basalt paving stones, a white marble elephant fountain in the centre, Sant'Agata Cathedral behind — Catania's Baroque heart. Between 07:00 and 09:00 the square is nearly empty: best light, fewest people, €1 espresso standing at the bar at the corner café. Afternoon brings the crowds. For photos: early morning. For sitting: late afternoon.

overview.title: Welcome to Catania

transport.intro: The historic centre is compact and everything is walkable. But know the single daily bus for Etna and Trenitalia for the rest of Sicily.

items.title: Airport → centre: 20 minutes on the Alibus
items.description: AMT Alibus runs from the airport to Catania Centrale station and Via Etnea in 20-25 minutes. Ticket €4 — from the machine at the airport or the driver, card accepted. Departures every 25 minutes, from 04:40 to midnight. Fixed-price taxi to the city centre ~€20-25. The Alibus is both cheap and reliable — hard to miss the stop.

items.title: AMT bus and metro — city transport
items.description: AMT city buses and a single-line metro. Ticket €1, valid 90 minutes, from tabacchi or edicole. When you board, don't forget to validate your ticket — inspectors appear without warning. The metro runs mainly northward; walking is more practical for the historic centre. AMT serves Ognina, Riviera dei Ciclopi and the beaches.

items.title: AST bus to Etna — the only daily service
items.description: AST bus departs Piazza Giovanni XXIII at 08:15, reaching Rifugio Sapienza (1,910 m) at 10:15. Return at 16:30. Return ticket €6.60, cash, from the driver. No other service. Miss it and there's no way up to Etna that day. Cable car to 2,500 m costs an additional ~€50. Cold and windy up top — jacket, water and sunscreen essential.

items.title: Train — the gateway to the rest of Sicily
items.description: From Catania Centrale on Trenitalia: Palermo ~3 hrs, Messina 1.5 hrs, Siracusa 1-1.5 hrs (€5-10), Agrigento ~2.5 hrs. The train to Siracusa is both cheap and scenic — ideal for a day trip. For Taormina, get off at Giardini-Naxos station and take a minibus or taxi up to the hilltop town.

items.title: Walking — all you need for the historic centre
items.description: From Piazza del Duomo: La Pescheria 2 minutes, Via Etnea 1 minute, Bellini Theatre 5 minutes, Roman Theatre 8 minutes, Via Crociferi 10 minutes. The entire historic centre can be covered in a comfortable morning walk. Watch for scooters in narrow streets and wet basalt after rain.

callout.label: Circumetnea — circling Etna on a train since 1898
callout.text: Departs from Catania Borgo station (not Catania Centrale — 1 km away) and circles Etna to reach Riposto in 3 hours. Lava flow traces, orange and lemon groves, volcanic villages. Ticket ~€8-10. For those who want to see around Etna rather than climb it — authentic and peaceful, but very limited Sunday service.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Catania's historic centre is so compact that wherever you stay, everything is walkable. The choice comes down to what sound you want to wake up to in the morning.

local_word.definition: The material that defines Catania's architecture and colour: the dark black basalt lava of Etna. The city destroyed by the 1693 earthquake was rebuilt from this stone — cathedrals, palaces, balconies, pavements. The contrast between black basalt and white Siracusa limestone is the visual signature of Catanian Baroque. After rain, wet lava stone photographs so beautifully that you end up grateful for cloudy mornings.

items.name: Around Piazza del Duomo
items.description: 2 minutes to La Pescheria, 1 minute to Via Etnea. At 06:30 you wake up to market sounds, fishermen's voices and coffee aromas — for that experience, a little noise is worth it. Boutique hotels and B&Bs available at reasonable prices.

items.name: Along Via Etnea
items.description: Catania's main shopping and passeggiata street. Cafés, restaurants, boutiques. Piazza Stesicoro and the Roman amphitheatre ruins are on this street. Walking north, you suddenly see Etna straight ahead — that perspective sums up Catania. Evening flow is lively.

items.name: San Cristoforo area
items.description: South-west of La Pescheria, a completely local and quiet neighbourhood. Almost no tourist pressure. This is Catania's afternoon rhythm: shopkeepers talking, children playing, nobody handing you an English menu.

items.name: Ognina — small fishing harbour
items.description: A quiet neighbourhood to the north built around a small fishing harbour. 15-20 minutes to the historic centre by AMT. Good fresh fish restaurants for evening meals. Etna looks wider from the north here.

items.name: Aci Trezza — at the foot of the Cyclops' rocks
items.description: 15-20 minutes from Catania by bus, but feels like a different world. A small fishing village at the foot of the basalt rocks from Homer's Odyssey. Fresh fish trattorias, evening sun and real Sicilian coastline. Good balance for those wanting to escape the city without leaving it too far.

items.name: Taormina — a different base
items.description: 50 minutes from Catania by bus or train. Ancient Greek theatre on a hilltop with Etna and sea views — magnificent but touristy. A morning Etna + evening Taormina plan is possible. Staying overnight in Taormina means seeing the town in its real state once the crowds leave.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: When you visit Catania directly determines your relationship with Etna. The volcano shows a different face every season — and the city changes with it.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Etna at its finest
items.description: April and May are the most balanced period for both Etna and the city. Temperatures 18-24°C — ideal for climbing, neither too hot nor icy. La Pescheria mornings at their most lively. Orange and lemon groves in their final harvest days. Crowds remain manageable through to mid-June.

callout.label: Etna climbing — when, how, how much?
callout.text: April-June and September-October are the best periods. AST bus to Rifugio Sapienza (1,910 m), cable car to 2,500 m (~€50). From there it's possible to walk up to 2,900 m. Reaching the active craters at 3,320 m requires a licensed guide — independent access is prohibited. Check the weather forecast before going: Etna closes suddenly, strong wind can halt cable car operations.

items.subtitle: Spring · Ideal conditions for Etna, citrus harvest ending, fewer crowds

items.label: Summer
items.name: Summer in a volcano's shadow
items.description: July and August are very hot — 35-38°C is normal. Etna climbing must be completed before midday. The city slows down at lunchtime and comes back alive after 19:00. The beaches of Riviera dei Ciclopi (Aci Trezza, Aci Castello) are the best cooling option during the day.

callout.label: Riviera dei Ciclopi — summer on Homer's shore
callout.text: Just north of Catania, 20-30 minutes by AMT. At Aci Castello, an 11th-century Norman castle juts directly into the sea. At Aci Trezza, the black basalt rocks said to be hurled by the Cyclops in the Odyssey rise from the Mediterranean. Both villages can be planned as a day trip — combined with fresh fish dinners, possibly Catania's finest summer day.

items.subtitle: Summer · 35-38°C, Etna is morning business, La Pescheria anchors the daily rhythm

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Blood oranges and a quieter Etna
items.description: September and October see the crowds thin, temperatures settle at 22-26°C and Etna climbing conditions return to ideal. Citrus season begins — blood oranges, mandarins, bergamot. La Pescheria mornings slightly quieter but still part of the morning ritual. November brings rain but prices drop noticeably.

callout.label: Blood orange season — November through February
callout.text: Sicily's Moro and Tarocco blood oranges grow in Etna's volcanic, mineral-rich soil — no other land produces this colour and depth of flavour. Harvest starts in November, peaking in January-February. Freshly squeezed blood orange juice at La Pescheria and Piazza Carlo Alberto market €1-2. Villages on Etna's southern slopes (Zafferana Etnea, Viagrande) are surrounded by orchards — worth stopping at on the Etna road.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Etna ideal again, citrus season beginning

items.label: Winter
items.name: Sant'Agata's city
items.description: From December to February Catania is quiet but alive in its own way. 3-5 February: Sant'Agata Festival — Sicily's largest religious celebration. Etna is under snow and climbing is not possible. Museums nearly empty, prices at their annual lowest. This winter period shows you the real Catania.

callout.label: Sant'Agata Festival — 3-5 February, around 1 million participants
callout.text: Every year on 3-5 February, one of Europe's great religious festivals recognised by the Vatican. Around a million participants: the great silver-reliquary procession, Catanians walking the streets in traditional white tunics, fireworks and prayers. For three days the city becomes something entirely different. If you want to catch this, book at least 3 months ahead — finding a hotel genuinely gets difficult.

items.subtitle: Winter · 3-5 February Sant'Agata Festival, blood oranges, empty museums and streets

best_time.title: When to Go

monthly_highlights.text: Festa di Sant'Agata: one of the world's biggest saint festivals — hundreds of thousands in white robes, night processions and sugar statues.
Sea + volcano season: Etna in the morning, La Playa or the Aci Trezza rocks in the afternoon; the city lives on the street at night.
Etna harvest: the volcano-slope wineries pick their grapes; chestnut, pistachio and new wine season.
Snow-capped Etna views: the summit turns white as orange season begins — the sweetest months for blood-orange juice.

eat.intro: Catania's cuisine is slightly more refined than Palermo's but equally generous and self-assured. Street food is morning business, fresh fish is midday, and Bellini's pasta belongs to the evening.

local_word.definition: Catania's greatest gift to Italian cuisine — fried aubergine, tomato sauce, grated salted ricotta and fresh basil. Served with penne or rigatoni. Named after the most famous opera by Catanian composer Vincenzo Bellini. Legend has it a Catanian chef first tasted it and exclaimed 'questa è una Norma!' — meaning 'this is a masterpiece!' Found in every restaurant in Catania, but the version made with freshly fried aubergine and quality salted ricotta is genuinely different.

items.name: Granita e brioche
items.description: Sicily's most original morning tradition and Catania's breakfast ritual. Semi-frozen granita — almond, pistachio, lemon, strawberry or mulberry — inside or alongside a warm buttery brioche. Fresh in every café from 07:00 to 10:00. Almond granita is the Catanian classic; from Caffè del Duomo or cafés on Via Etnea, €3-5.
items.tag: Every café · €3–5 · 07:00–10:00 · almond granita the Catanian classic

items.name: Arancino
items.description: Catania's pointed, pyramid-shaped fried rice ball — filled with meat ragù, peas and egg. In every café and bakery for €1.50-3. Can be eaten for breakfast, at lunch or while walking. Here it's called arancino, masculine and pointed — call it arancina and you're confusing it with Palermo's version.
items.tag: Every bakery and café · €1.50–3 · ragù filling is classic · fresh in the morning

items.name: Pasta alla Norma
items.description: The pasta Catania invented and Italy adopted. Fresh fried aubergine, intense tomato sauce, grated salted ricotta and basil. Ingredient quality determines everything — reheated aubergine or aged ricotta is a disappointment. Trattorias around Via Crociferi and the back streets off Piazza del Duomo: €8-12.
items.tag: Local trattorias · €8–12 · freshly fried aubergine essential

items.name: Fresh fish — from La Pescheria to your table
items.description: Lunch at the small trattorias surrounding La Pescheria is both the freshest and most affordable option. Swordfish (pesce spada) is Catania's symbol — one of the finest varieties from these Mediterranean waters. Octopus, mussels and sea urchin also in abundance. Seafood portions €12-20. Go at midday — fresh stock runs out by evening.
items.tag: Around La Pescheria · €12–20 · go at midday · swordfish is the classic

items.name: Scacciata and pizzolo
items.description: Catania's own street food, not found in Palermo. Scacciata: a closed flatbread baked with cabbage and sausage or potato and cheese filling between two layers of dough. Pizzolo: Catania's double-layered stone-oven pizza. Both work for lunch and dinner. From small bakeries and rosticcerias, €3-6.
items.tag: Small bakeries and rosticcerias · €3–6 · lunch and dinner

items.name: Cannolo and cassata
items.description: Sicilian pastry heritage at its finest in Catania. Cannolo: fried pastry tube, fresh ricotta filling, candied fruit and pistachio. Cassata: sponge cake, ricotta cream, green marzipan and candied fruit. Fresh ricotta is the critical point in both — don't accept day-old ricotta. Pasticceria Savia on Via Etnea, in the same spot since 1897. €2-4.
items.tag: Pasticceria Savia, Via Etnea · €2–4 · fresh ricotta essential

callout.label: Piazza Carlo Alberto — La Fera, the Sunday alternative
callout.text: La Pescheria is closed on Sundays — but on Sundays north of Via Etnea at Piazza Carlo Alberto, the La Fera weekly market sets up from 07:00 to 13:00. Clothing to toys, local spices to Etna products. Cheap, crowded and very local. Good source for blood oranges, almonds, lemons and Sicilian olive oil.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Understanding Catania requires going beyond Piazza del Duomo. The city's soul is hidden in the very early hours, on Etna's slopes or on the shore Homer described.

items.name: Etna
items.description: AST bus from the south to Rifugio Sapienza (1,910 m), then cable car to 2,500 m (~€50). Active craters at 3,320 m — licensed guide mandatory, independent access prohibited. But even the view at 2,500 m takes your breath away: Catania and the Sicilian coast spread out below, lava fields alongside. Don't miss the 08:15 bus — it's the only one.
items.rarity: The neighbour looking through your window every morning — the world's most active volcano

items.name: La Pescheria
items.description: Down the steps right behind Piazza del Duomo, La Pescheria begins. Open 06:00-13:00, closed Sundays. Squid, sea urchin, swordfish, octopus — vendors shouting in Sicilian dialect, everything laid on ice. Ask before taking photos — most vendors are happy. Lunch at the trattorias surrounding the market is both the freshest and cheapest option.
items.rarity: 07:00 in the morning — fish, shouting, Sicilian scents and time frozen

items.name: Teatro Massimo Bellini and Via Crociferi
items.description: Vincenzo Bellini (1801-1835) was born in Catania and his most famous opera Norma premiered here. Teatro Massimo Bellini is both opera house and museum — worth seeing inside. Via Crociferi is the city's most beautiful Baroque street: four churches in succession, narrow lava-paved road, climbing plants. Nearly empty early in the morning. Sant'Benedetto Monastery on this street — its interior is magnificent and rarely crowded.
items.rarity: Bellini was born here — and the city reminds you at every corner

items.name: Aci Trezza and Aci Castello
items.description: 15-20 minutes from Catania by bus, but it feels like arriving somewhere entirely different. At Aci Trezza, the black basalt rocks known as the Cyclops' stones rise from the sea — the very rocks Homer says Polyphemos hurled at Odysseus in the Odyssey. Small fishing village, evening sun and extraordinary fresh fish trattorias. At Aci Castello, a Norman castle sits directly on the rock, reaching into the sea. Both together make a full day.
items.rarity: Homer passed through here — the rocks have stood in the same place for 3,000 years

items.name: Piazza Stesicoro — Roman amphitheatre remains
items.description: On Via Etnea, in the middle of Piazza Stesicoro, the remains of a Roman amphitheatre are visible beneath the pavement. Behind a protective fence, in the open air, free. Believed to date from the 2nd century with a capacity of around 15,000. Etna visible in the same frame from the nearby Belvedere. The most tangible evidence of the history the city was built on top of.
items.rarity: 2,000 years under the pavement — and almost nobody stops to look

items.name: Etna's blood orange groves
items.description: Around Catania, Etna's volcanic, mineral-rich soil produces the world's finest blood oranges. From November to March, freshly squeezed blood orange juice at the markets for €1-2. The colour is deep red with wine tones, the taste complex and intense. Villages on Etna's southern slopes (Zafferana Etnea, Viagrande) sit among these orchards — worth stopping at on the Etna road if travelling by car.
items.rarity: Sicily's blood orange — no other soil produces this colour and flavour anywhere

callout.label: Monastero dei Benedettini — Catania's least-known major building
callout.text: Right near Via Crociferi at Piazza Dante. One of Europe's largest Benedictine monasteries, now partly housing the University of Catania. Inside: large courtyards, a historic library, a magnificent Baroque staircase. Guided tours available and genuinely worthwhile — they reveal details that independent visitors miss. A building of impressive scale and architecture that the tourist flow rarely reaches.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Start the day with granita e brioche
items.sub: Every café, 07:00-10:00. Almond granita is classic. €3-5. This breakfast sets the tone for Catania.

items.label: Get to La Pescheria at 07:00
items.sub: Behind Piazza del Duomo, down the steps. Closed Sundays. Swordfish, sea urchin, octopus.

items.label: Don't miss the 08:15 bus to Etna
items.sub: AST from Piazza Giovanni XXIII. €6.60 return, cash. Bring a jacket and water. Cable car extra ~€50.

items.label: Eat pasta alla Norma
items.sub: Local trattoria. €8-12. Freshly fried aubergine and salted ricotta essential. Catania's own invention.

items.label: See Piazza del Duomo early in the morning
items.sub: 07:00-09:00 nearly empty. Elephant fountain, black-and-white Baroque façade, Sant'Agata Cathedral.

items.label: Walk Via Crociferi
items.sub: Catania's finest Baroque street. Four churches in a row. Go inside Sant'Benedetto Monastery.

items.label: Eat arancino — pointed, masculine
items.sub: Every bakery and café. €1.50-3. Ragù filling is the classic. Don't call it arancina — that's Palermo's name.

items.label: Go to Aci Trezza
items.sub: AMT bus 15-20 min. The Cyclops' rocks, fresh fish trattoria, spectacular evening sun.

items.label: Look at the Roman amphitheatre remains at Piazza Stesicoro
items.sub: On Via Etnea. Visible beneath the pavement. Free. Little known, very impressive.

items.label: Visit Monastero dei Benedettini
items.sub: Piazza Dante. Guided tours available. Few crowds. Impressive scale and Baroque architecture.

items.label: Drink blood orange juice — the fresh version
items.sub: November-March is best. €1-2. Deep red, complex taste. The world's finest grown here.

items.label: Eat cannolo — from Pasticceria Savia
items.sub: On Via Etnea. In the same spot since 1897. €2-4. Fresh ricotta essential — don't accept day-old.

checklist.title: Catania Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Leaving Catania, Etna is still behind you — and you're making a promise to climb to the active craters next time.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Catania is an honest city built of lava stone; its traps are few, but a few games run in the volcano's shadow. These four suffice.

items.name: 'Etna jeep tours' sold on the street
items.description: The brochure-waving 'tour sellers' on the squares sell a mediocre minibus ride as a summit tour; unauthorised trips to the crater zone are dangerous besides.
items.instead: Do Etna by cable car + authorised guide, or with known operators' sunrise/sunset tours; the mountain demands seriousness.

items.name: Fish with the kilo price unasked by the Pescheria
items.description: Some restaurants around the market say 'fresh fish' and reveal the per-kilo price afterwards; the bill becomes a surprise.
items.instead: Ask the weight and the price before ordering; or pick the small eateries that cook what you buy from the market stalls.

items.name: Going up to Taormina at noon in August
items.description: The coast road and Taormina's car parks lock up at summer midday; the terrace town becomes a selfie queue.
items.instead: Take the first morning train to Taormina or go late afternoon; save midday for Catania's shaded courtyards.

items.name: Ready-made granita at a tourist bar
items.description: Industrial-syrup 'granita' is an insult to this city; the real thing is handmade and fresh each morning.
items.instead: Drink it at the historic pastry shops (try almond + coffee mixed), with a warm brioche col tuppo — the constitution of a Catania breakfast.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Everything in Catania is set to Etna's clock: the mountain is clear in the morning and clouds over by noon. Rise early to see the volcano; go to the market to understand the city.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the fish market to the lava-stone streets

steps.title: La Pescheria
steps.description: Shouting vendors, swordfish heads, the smell of ice and lemon: the Mediterranean's most theatrical market peaks early.

steps.title: Granita e brioche breakfast
steps.description: Almond granita + warm brioche: Sicily's breakfast constitution. Summer or winter, no difference.

steps.title: Piazza del Duomo + the elephant
steps.description: The lava-stone elephant (u Liotru) is the city's talisman; visit Bellini's tomb in the cathedral.

steps.title: Via Crociferi + Via Etnea
steps.description: From the street of baroque churches to the city's spine: windows, courtyards, and Etna always on the horizon.

steps.title: Lunch — pasta alla Norma
steps.description: The pasta named after Bellini's opera tastes different in its birthplace; an Etna white alongside.

steps.title: Aci Trezza late afternoon
steps.description: The seafront opposite the rocks the Cyclops threw; granita or aperitivo at sunset, dinner back in Catania.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The city classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: market, granita, Duomo, Crociferi, Aci Trezza.

steps.title: Etna day
steps.description: Early cable car + guided crater zone (windbreaker mandatory, even in summer); a honey-and-pistachio stop in Zafferana on the way down, and a tired, happy pizza at night.

steps.title: Taormina or deep Catania
steps.description: Either the first train to Taormina: the ancient theatre + Isola Bella; or stay urban: the Roman ruins of Piazza Stesicoro, Ursino Castle, a farewell cannolo.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Italian opens doors; Sicilian gets laughs. With these five you can even haggle at the market.

items.meaning: Hi / bye — any hour, to anyone
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — Etna wine glasses rise to this
Sicilian for 'wow!' — it escapes by itself the first time you see Etna
